q: token_counter.rs loads the CoreBPE tokenizer into a `static TOKENIZER: OnceCell<Arc<CoreBPE>>` because:
options: Tokenizer loading is expensive startup work paid once per process, shared by all counters
The tokenizer is not thread-safe and must be hidden behind OnceCell
OnceCell guarantees the tokenizer updates when models change
static storage makes tokenization faster per message by 10x automatically
explanation: Arc<CoreBPE> is chosen precisely for shared, thread-safe access.
OnceCell is write-once; it never updates data.
Static storage alone does not change per-message cost; avoiding re-loading does.

q: The token cache key is `(len, blake3 hash)` rather than the raw text. Why?
options: Identical content matches without storing giant strings in the key — bounded memory for the cache itself
Hashes are faster to tokenize than strings
Rust cannot compare strings in HashMap keys
The tokenizer only accepts hashed input
explanation: Hashing is the identity check, not a faster tokenization path.
String keys in HashMaps are idiomatic and fine.
The tokenizer consumes real text; hashing is for the cache layer only.

options: Cache memory is finite — unbounded caches swap compute savings for memory amnesia
The tokenizer cannot exceed 1,024 distinct outputs
Hashing more than 1,024 strings per session is a security violation
LRU structures in Rust are capped by the language
explanation: Tokenizer output variety is unbounded in principle; the cache is the bounded part.
No security rule keys on hash counts.
LRU caps come from design (NonZeroUsize), not language limits.

q: A tool returns 500,000 chars of text. Per large_response_handler's contract, the agent receives:
options: A pointer message naming a temp file where the bulk was spilled
The full text, since 500k chars fits in most contexts
The first 200,000 chars only
An error refusing the tool result
explanation: The threshold is 200,000 chars — 500k exceeds it and gets spilled.
Truncation would lose data; the handler keeps everything on disk instead.
The result is not refused; it is relocated and summarized.

q: `GOOSE_CONTEXT_LIMIT = 0` in config is an error state because:
options: Zero would silently amputate sessions; the value must be a usize greater than 0
Zero is not a valid type for a usize
The config file rejects all numeric strings
Zero conflicts with the default 200,000 threshold naming
explanation: 0 is a perfectly valid usize — it's rejected by validation, not by typing.
Numeric config strings parse fine; the check is value-based.
The 200k threshold belongs to tool responses, unrelated to context limit.

q: The performance lesson from `e7c33077c fix: secure large response spill files` plus the handler's design together say:
options: Bounding resources (spill threshold, temp file) is BOTH a perf and a security concern — one mechanism serves both
Perf work and security work must never touch the same file
Large responses should be rejected to avoid all risk
Spill files make context tracking unnecessary
explanation: The same handler serves both: the fix history proves they are coupled, not separable.
Rejecting large responses breaks real tool workflows; relocation preserves them.
Context tracking still applies to the pointer message; spilling is not an exemption.

q: Fix this memory mistake: a contributor 'optimizes' the token cache by unbounded `HashMap::new()` growth keyed on every distinct prompt. The problem a reviewer must flag:
options: Unbounded cache = unbounded memory; retain the LRU bound (1,024) so hot entries churn but RAM stays flat
HashMaps are slower than LruCache for any size
Distinct prompts must never be cached at all
The tokenizer requires a cache to be present to load
explanation: Map performance is fine; the issue is unbounded residency.
Caching distinct prompts is the whole point of the identity-key design.
The tokenizer loads independently; the cache is an optimization layer.
